https://www.politico.eu/article/german-d.text: German Defense Minister Boris Pistorius will meet with the Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth in Washington this month, a surprising shift after the Pentagon chief rebuffed a visit earlier this year. The meeting will take place as part of Pistorius’ trip to the U.S. for a rollout of F-35 warplanes purchased by Germany, according to two NATO defense officials and a U.S. defense official familiar with the planning, who were granted anonymity to discuss a sensitive topic. The talks are significant given Hegseth’s earlier snub amid tensions between the two countries over the wars in Iran and Ukraine. Advertisement Advertisement Relations have been frosty between the two countries and may have factored into Hegseth’s earlier decision not to meet with Pistorius. President Donald Trump ordered the withdrawal of 5,000 troops from Germany in May after German President Friederich Merz criticized the U.S. war with Iran. The repositioning of the troops is expected to take up to a year to complete. It’s likely the two men will discuss a recent attempted Russian drone attack at an airport in Germany at their Sept. 15 meeting, as well as a Pentagon review of the U.S. military presence in Europe. The Trump administration is weighing a variety of options, including significant troop reductions on the continent. Germany could feel the brunt of any reductions, given the tens of thousands of Americans stationed there along with several large bases and training ranges. Pistorius will travel to the U.S. for a rollout ceremony in Texas for the first F-35 fighter jets scheduled for delivery to the German armed forces. Germany still remains a major contributor to NATO and is one of Europe’s biggest buyers of U.S. weapons, including the order of 35 F-35 fighter planes and a significant purchase of eight P-8 surveillance aircraft, the first of which have already been delivered. Germany is one of just a handful of American allies to buy the advanced submarine hunting plane, which will allow the Germany navy to assume a larger role in tracking Russian submarines and monitoring undersea cables and infrastructure in the Baltic and North Atlantic. Advertisement Advertisement There is increasing worry in Europe that Russia will attack that undersea infrastructure given Moscow’s desire to lash out at Europe for supporting Ukraine. An explosives-laden drone was recently discovered at an airport in Leipzig, and the German government said the device was made by Russia. Hegseth and Pistorius met previously, at the NATO summit in Turkey in July and last summer during a visit at the Pentagon. Several months after those meetings, the Trump administration approved the sale of long-range Tomahawk cruise missiles to Germany. There are 38,000 U.S. troops stationed in Germany, which also serves as the home base for U.S. European and Africa commands. It’s the largest deployment of American forces in Europe.

Play Video Article content Never mind that Cope’s victim, his girlfriend, whom he had savagely beaten in the street, was also Indigenous and that by discounting Cope’s sentence from five years to three the judge was indirectly declaring that crimes against Indigenous women are less serious. Then there was an Ontario offender, Temidayo Olasusi, who was convicted of eight counts of abusing and sexually trafficking an Indigenous woman. Olasusi had 13 convictions stretching back to 2013, including possession of child pornography. But he was given a pre-sentence Impact of Race and Culture Assessment, which concluded that although he grew up in a stable, successful home, he had “experienced anti-Black racism.” The judge acknowledged that there was no connection between that racism and Olasusi’s offences, but he discounted Olasusi’s sentence anyway by more than half. Article content A non-citizen of Canada, Czech Marek Grundza, who has permanent residence status, used his car to run down a police officer and leave the officer dying at the side of a road. But because Grundza faced deportation if he received significant prison time (what the judge in his case called “collateral immigration consequence”) Grnudza was given only house arrest. Guess it’s open season on cops, too. The list of race-based sentencing goes on and on. Tristin Hopper of the National Post found 15 such cases in just 15 court days between Sept. 23 and Oct. 15. So, what Alberta provincial court judge Steven Bilodeau did last week was a refreshing tonic against sentencing insanity. Back in May, Shaye Riley Bird, an Indigenous man, plead guilty to the unprovoked stabbing of a complete stranger during a mugging on an Edmonton street. Both Bird’s defence council and the Crown prosecutor submitted a joint sentencing recommendation of six months in jail because while the victim suffered a serious wound to a buttock he was otherwise unhurt. Article content Judge Bilodeau, in a surprisingly frank judgement, called the joint recommendation “unhinged.” Rather than giving Bird six months of jail time, the judge upped it to 18 months. The reasons Justice Bilodeau gave for overriding the joint submission are clear enough. “First, it does not adequately reflect the gravity of this random group attack with a knife. Second, it gives no meaningful effect to the serious and lasting impact upon the victim. Third, the proposed concurrent sentence leaves the separate breach of the weapons condition without any meaningful sanction.” When Bird was released from jail in March of this year, his release conditions included a ban on possessing weapons. Judge Bilodeau reasoned, correctly, that if the sentence for breaching conditions was rolled in with Bird’s other conviction for assault causing bodily harm, that would render the breach for possessing a knife meaningless. What makes this sentence even more surprising is that the court is required by Canadian law to consider what are called Gladue factors because Bird is an Indigenous man. If there is any way at all to reduce an Indigenous person’s sentence, it must be reduced because of the historic mistreatment of Indigenous people, the discrimination they are currently subjected to, the high percentage of inmates who are Indigenous and the lingering cultural impact of residential schools and family separations. Article content It can be debated whether even 18 months is long enough for a violent, unprovoked attack on a stranger minding his own business on a public sidewalk. But at least this one case defies the recent trend of Canadian courts.
